Family Health

Cauda equina syndrome: emergency symptoms, treatment and recovery

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

New bladder or bowel difficulties, altered feeling around the genitals or anus, or progressing leg weakness can signal a spinal emergency. Seek immediate assessment rather than waiting to see whether the symptoms settle.

What the cauda equina does

The spinal cord ends above a bundle of nerve roots that continues through the lower spinal canal. Its name, cauda equina, comes from its resemblance to a horse’s tail. These nerves carry messages between the nervous system, legs and pelvic organs. They contribute to movement, sensation, bladder and bowel control and sexual function.

Cauda equina syndrome, often shortened to CES, occurs when these nerve roots stop functioning normally, commonly because something compresses them. It is rare, but the consequences can be serious. Untreated compression may leave lasting weakness, numbness or problems with continence. A rare condition still needs urgent consideration when its warning signs appear; a population estimate cannot tell you whether your own symptoms are safe.

New bladder, bowel or saddle changes are an emergency

Go to an emergency department immediately for new difficulty starting or controlling urination, loss of the feeling of urine flowing, inability to tell when the bladder is full, or new leakage together with concerning back or nerve symptoms. Retention means urine is not emptying properly. It can eventually cause overflow leakage, so being able to leak urine does not prove the bladder is working normally.

Other warning signs include altered sensation around the genitals, inner thighs, buttocks or anus, such as a different feeling when wiping; loss of bowel control or the usual feeling of needing to pass stool; and new sexual sensation or function changes. This region is often called the saddle area. Do not wait for every symptom, complete numbness or incontinence before seeking assessment.

Back and leg symptoms may accompany the pelvic changes

Severe lower back pain, pain travelling into one or both legs, leg weakness or numbness and altered reflexes may occur. Symptoms can appear abruptly or evolve, and their severity varies. A clinician checks the overall pattern rather than deciding from pain intensity alone. Walking normally, having symptoms on only one side or lacking severe back pain does not safely exclude CES.

Ordinary back pain is much more common than CES. Nevertheless, new saddle or bladder changes should never be dismissed as an expected part of sciatica. Tell emergency staff exactly what has changed and when it started. If symptoms progress while you are waiting, say so. If you cannot travel safely, use your local emergency number rather than driving with significant weakness or numbness.

A large disc herniation is a common cause

Discs cushion the bones of the spine. A disc has a softer centre within a tougher outer layer; when material protrudes through a weakened area, it may press on nearby nerves. A large herniation in the lower back can compress several cauda equina roots. Age-related changes or a lifting or twisting event may contribute, but many people cannot identify a single injury that caused it.

Other possible causes include spinal tumours or other lesions, infection or inflammation, a narrowed spinal canal, congenital differences, bleeding, major injury and complications after spinal surgery. A fall or vehicle collision therefore matters in the history. Treatment must address the actual cause; it is not always the same operation for every person with similar symptoms.

Risk factors do not replace an assessment

A previous disc problem may make a new episode of back and leg symptoms easier to recognise, but most people with disc herniation do not develop CES. Family history, body weight and jobs involving repeated heavy lifting, pushing, bending or twisting may be relevant to disc health. Repetitive loading in sport can also matter. None of these factors diagnoses CES or determines whether it will happen.

People without these risk factors can still develop compression. Avoid blaming yourself for a particular movement or assuming that a young, active person cannot be affected. When seeking help, mention previous spinal surgery, cancer, infection, injury and medicines, including blood thinners, as well as the new symptoms. Collecting a complete medical record should not delay emergency care.

Examination and urgent imaging help find the cause

The team will ask about symptom onset, progression, bladder emptying, bowel sensation and sexual function. Examination may include leg strength, sensation, reflexes and walking, if safe. You may be asked to stand, sit, raise a leg, move the back or walk on heels and toes. An intimate examination may be discussed with your consent and an appropriate chaperone. No single movement or examination finding can rule out the condition at home.

An urgent lumbar MRI is usually the key scan for identifying nerve compression. A bladder scan may help assess retained urine, but must be interpreted alongside the other findings. In selected circumstances specialists may use CT or CT myelography. A myelogram involves contrast around the spinal nerves followed by imaging; it is not a routine substitute chosen by the patient or a reason to postpone the urgent pathway.

Why treatment should not wait for a time limit

When compressive CES is confirmed, urgent surgery is commonly needed to relieve pressure and protect the remaining nerve function. Depending on the findings, a surgeon may remove protruding disc material, part of the bone around the canal or another compressing lesion. Infection, tumour or bleeding may require additional treatment from the relevant specialists.

You may see references to surgery within 24 to 48 hours. This is not a safe period to wait at home, nor a guarantee of recovery if surgery happens within it. Seek assessment immediately and let the spinal team decide timing. If symptoms have already lasted longer, care is still urgent and treatment may still help. Do not assume that a missed window makes assessment pointless.

Recovery includes movement and everyday activities

After surgery, follow-up checks wound healing and changes in strength, sensation, pain and continence. Some people recover well; others have persistent difficulties despite prompt treatment. Different functions can recover at different rates. Improvement may continue over months or longer, and bladder recovery can lag behind improvement in leg movement. A fixed recovery date cannot be promised.

Physiotherapy can support walking, strength and safe movement. Occupational therapy can help with dressing, transfers, home arrangements and other daily activities. Ask for written instructions about lifting, driving, work, exercise and wound care. New or worsening saddle, bladder or leg symptoms after treatment need urgent reassessment, even if earlier symptoms had begun to improve.

Pain treatment needs an individual medicine plan

Postoperative pain may need short-term prescription medicine, sometimes an opioid such as oxycodone. Ongoing nerve pain may require a different approach. Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, and anti-inflammatory medicines such as ibuprofen are not suitable for everyone or automatically appropriate for daily long-term use. Kidney or stomach problems, other medicines, pregnancy and the operation itself can affect the choice.

Steroids are not a routine self-treatment for every case of CES. Use them only when the treating team has a specific reason. Ask how long each medicine is intended for and which side effects to report. Constipation, sleepiness and effects on urination can complicate recovery. Do not increase doses or combine products without checking their ingredients and the discharge plan.

Bladder and bowel care should protect more than continence

Specialist bladder care aims for safe storage and effective emptying as well as fewer leaks. Some people need an indwelling catheter temporarily; others learn intermittent catheterisation on an individual schedule. Bladder training is suitable only when the team recommends it. Trying to hold urine longer or straining to force it out is not a general solution for nerve-related retention.

Medicines such as oxybutynin or tolterodine may help selected overactive-bladder problems but can worsen retention or constipation. Hyoscyamine is likewise not a default treatment for all CES bladder or bowel symptoms. Bowel care may include planned timing, diet and prescribed laxatives or suppositories, including glycerin when appropriate. A rehabilitation or continence team should design the routine rather than relying on a list of medicines.

Living with ongoing symptoms and getting support

If continence has not fully returned, absorbent pads, protective underwear and skin care may make daily life easier while treatment continues. Follow the catheter-care and fluid plan you are given. Drinking excessive water is not a guarantee against urinary infection; seek advice about fever, feeling unwell, new pain or a change in urinary symptoms. Longer-term follow-up may include checks on bladder and kidney function.

Changes in mobility, continence or sexual function can affect confidence, relationships and work. Psychological support, rehabilitation and sexual-health advice can be useful alongside medical treatment. Involve a partner, friend or relative if you want their help, while keeping control over what you share. Accepting support does not mean that treatable symptoms should be ignored or that you must manage the impact alone.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Suspected cauda equina syndrome needs immediate emergency assessment.

Urgent imaging and the spinal team guide treatment; a 24-to-48-hour figure is not permission to wait.

Recovery and bladder, bowel and pain treatment vary with the nerve injury and its cause.

How BeMama can help

Write down when each change began and describe bladder emptying and saddle sensation clearly. After treatment, keep one shared discharge and rehabilitation plan.

When to seek help

New saddle numbness, difficulty passing urine, loss of bladder or bowel control, or worsening leg weakness needs emergency assessment, including after spinal surgery.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Do not wait for complete incontinence or every warning sign.
  • An MRI usually helps identify compression.
  • Urgent treatment can still help after symptoms have been present for some time.
  • Continence, mobility and emotional support belong in the recovery plan.

Frequently asked questions

Does cauda equina mean the end of the spinal cord itself?

It names the bundle of nerve roots that continues below the end of the cord, supplying the legs and pelvic organs.

Can leaking urine happen when the bladder cannot empty?

Yes. An overfull bladder can leak. New leakage does not rule out retention or the need for urgent assessment.

Must both legs be affected?

No. The pattern varies. New bladder, bowel or saddle changes should be assessed even when symptoms are one-sided.

Can I wait until the 48-hour point?

No. Seek emergency assessment immediately. A reported surgical timing window is not a safe waiting period.

Is it too late to get help after two days?

No. Urgent assessment is still necessary and treatment may still help. Do not decide that care is pointless.

Will a normal movement test exclude CES?

No. No home movement check can exclude it. Clinicians assess the history and examination and arrange appropriate imaging.

Does surgery guarantee full recovery?

No. It relieves compression and protects nerve function, but recovery is variable and some difficulties persist.

Should everyone take oxybutynin or tolterodine?

No. These medicines help selected bladder problems and may worsen retention. The bladder pattern must be assessed first.

Can I simply drink more water to prevent infection?

Follow your individual fluid and catheter-care plan. Excess water does not guarantee protection and does not correct poor emptying.

Who can help with the longer-term effects?

Rehabilitation, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, continence and sexual-health services and psychological support can each address different needs.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
